utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning. Anna Richterova for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with David Cunningham and Vesna Anic today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. If there is agreement on your part - and when I say your part, it means both sides, obviously - there is the possibility of us sitting until the end of the month or until the 27th of June, always in the morning, if that is agreeable with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, it is agreeable with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see you nod, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is one thing that basically that would mean we would shift for the entire month, bar one day, to courtroom 3, but if we are moving to courtroom 3, what would have been court maintenance day on the 27th of June, being court maintenance day for courtroom 2, where we would have been sitting, would no longer be applicable to us. So I am suggesting, although we still have to decide ourselves as well, that we also sit on the 27th of June. That would be an extra day. I would like to know whether you agree with this as well. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'd suggest that on the 27th of June, we sit here in courtroom 2, Your Honour, if it's available. Actually, those days are really important, especially since we're going to go straight through to August and I have almost no support staff at this point, and I'm -- you might some day -- sometime day get a chance to read a letter I sent to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was reading through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's becoming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll come to it. I'll come to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's becoming a very serious problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll come to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A day of ability to get caught up sure is helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We would like to sit all the days because of course every day is very precious to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I admire your sense of dedication, Madam Richterova, and your enthusiasm to work every day, like the rest of us. So we'll come back to you on this 27th of June later on. But the probability is that we will sit that extra day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the Registry would assign me three more lawyers like the Prosecutor has, we can sit every day and afternoons and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next, then we also have the possibility -- and again my recommendation supported by my two colleagues is in the positive. The week 30th June to 4th July, we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon in another courtroom, in courtroom 1 or courtroom 3. I am proposing to you that we sit that week in the morning, we shift to the morning, but we will be sitting in this courtroom, courtroom 2. So that would be an entire week in courtroom 2. If that is acceptable to you. Otherwise, we stay in the afternoon and we sit where we are scheduled to sit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We prefer sitting in the mornings, so we do not object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next thing is I received a copy of a letter by Mr. Ackerman, addressed to the acting director of OLAD, Ms. Monica Martinez. I haven't read it all as yet, because it was only handed to me prior to the beginning of this sitting. I will go through it. My recommendation at this point in time is that I would believe that the letter and your request will carry much more weight, Mr. Ackerman, if you have the explicit support of the Prosecution, which you have had in the past. So if you can combine efforts towards the direction where you were heading, I think there is a better chance; otherwise, you know that the office concerned is pretty much tight within the parameters set by the exigencies -- several exigencies of this Tribunal, plus practice in other cases. I can promise you I will lend my support and that of my colleagues, because we realise that every Defence, every accused must have -- should have an adequate defence available. But before we speak out, I would rather await to see what reaction there's going to be from Ms. Martinez and also whether there's going to be this support from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave you a copy of the communication as a courtesy, after I noticed that every time Ms. Martinez was writing to me about resources, she was sending a copy to you, and so I decided I would -- I should do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very rarely, actually, I got copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, her most recent communication regarding Mr. Maglov, for instance, I noticed was copied to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was copied. Yes. And again, I mean, you may be -- you may have every good reason in the world to argue that the rate of 15 Euros is not adequate, but at the same time, if that is the rate that they apply to someone who is not yet a graduate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or 25 Euros. I don't know how much it was. 25 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, every request has to be tabled within the parameters which apply to that particular office. Don't forget that there are controls that are put in place here, and inspectors that come and make sure that the rates are being applied, et cetera, plus there are other things in the offing which would regulate precisely the remuneration that would be applicable. So what I can promise you, Mr. Ackerman, is that you can count on our support for whatever appears to us to be reasonable. What is definitely reasonable is that you need to be in a position defend your client adequately. So whatever you need ought to be given to you, especially considering that this is not an easy case or a normal case. It's a heavily laden case, complicated, already one year and a half old almost, with thousands of pages of documents, et cetera. So I'll wait to hear for some kind of response from the Prosecution, and also try to get updated from -- by OLAD, and then we shall take the stand that we will consider most appropriate, keeping in mind the principle that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted you to all understand that I'm not making a specific request of the Chamber at this point, but simply providing you with a courtesy copy. The other thing I'll mention regarding the 15 Euro rate, that is a rate that's based upon the entry-level position for, for instance, a case manager for the Prosecutor's office, the lowest level, and that is not a person who is skilled in -- who is multilingual, skilled in B/C/S, and able to translate and interpret the language. So we're -- the skill level of the person we're looking for is dramatically different. I've asked a number of people who are here in The Hague if they know anyone who would be willing to work for 15 Euros an hour, 150 hours a month in this case, and the response I mostly get is laughter, because nobody is going to work for that kind of money. They can command significantly more money if they have the language skills that are needed for this particular job. So I think the Registry is simply behind times with regard to the rate, behind the economy, and I just don't think we're going to get anyone if we can't do something about that. You know, who knows somebody may appear tomorrow and say they'll do it, but I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, I will take into account what you have written, and we'll come back to you, particularly after we've found out exactly what the situation is. So I understand the next witness enjoys some protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness was granted protective measures of facial distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym, BT64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So before we start and before we bring him in, do we need to put the screen or we just keep the public out? In this courtroom I think we would keep the public out, no?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the public is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And there is I suppose no filming while the witness is coming in?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. Okay. Next thing is may I remind everyone, please, Prosecution, Registry staff, Defence, Accused, and ourselves, of course, to keep your microphones switched off when the witness is speaking. All right? Thanks. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will soon be giving evidence, and before you do so, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a document that is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Now, don't talk unless I tell you to, okay? I will be explaining to you a few things before you start giving evidence. For reasons that you pointed out to the Prosecution and which were pointed out to us, we have decided to grant you certain protective measures. I don't know if these have been explained to you. If they haven't, or even if they have, I'm going to explain them to you. You will not be referred to here in the course of these proceedings by your name, but you are going to be given a number, which is BT90 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is BT64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BT64. You are going to be known and referred to as BT64. So no one outside these four walls will know your name or that you have testified in these proceedings. Then you asked for, and we have granted, that although the proceedings will be transmitted live, as they usually are, no one will be able to see your image. Your face, in other words, your appearance, is distorted, and if you look at the screen, at the video screen - and I ask the camera to point towards the witness - you will see how others will see you. No one will see your face. That's what they will see. And that's also because you asked for this kind of protective measure. Last but not least, you asked for your voice not to be heard naturally. So what we are going to do is we are going to distort your voice. So what others will hear is not your voice, but distortion of your voice. That way, we have tried to do our utmost to protect your identity. Does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the procedure that follows is the following: Madam Richterova, who you certainly have met already, will be asking you a series of questions. She will then be followed by Mr. Cunningham, I suppose, who is one of the lawyers appearing for Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this trial, who will also ask you a series of questions, which we call cross-examination. My duty as the Presiding Judge is to draw your attention to a very important principle, namely, that it is your duty, your obligation, to answer every question that is put to you, irrespective of where it is coming from, whether it's the Prosecution or the Defence, as fully and as truthfully as possible. You have no right to make any distinction between questions forthcoming from the Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. Everyone has a right to ask you questions here, including the Defence, and you have a duty to answer each and every question to the best of your ability, unless I personally tell you: Don't answer this question, in which case you don't answer the question that is put to you. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So having said that, I invite Ms. Richterova to start with her examination-in-chief. Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, sir, and I have to apologise that you have to wait for such a long time. Sir, I am going to show you a piece of paper on which your name is stated, and please confirm, just stating yes or no, whether you can see your name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1893, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go to private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for the first part of the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during 1991, are you ever at any rallies which would be organised only by one ethnicity, either Bosniaks or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Bosniaks and Serbs organised rallies in relation to the founding of the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after foundings of parties, were there some other rallies? And now I am referring to the year of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: In my village, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, in some other villages, were there any rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the Teslic municipality, in all the villages, there were rallies that were held, in relation to the founding of the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just -- you already said that it was in connection with founding these parties. Now I am asking you later, after the parties were established, in 1991, before the war in Croatia started, or after the war in Croatia started, were there any rallies held by one of the ethnicities, some big which would struck your attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead him, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that you learned about a big rally in the village of Cecava.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn about this rally? Who organised it? Who visited this rally? And were you present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, I was not present there, but there was transport that was organised for the village of Cecava, where rallies were held. It was a very large rally, and from all the -- for the people from all the parts of the municipality of Teslic, where there were Serbs, and Mr. Krajisnik attended this rally. According to a Serb, Dusan Vukovic, that's what he told me - this man told me this. I was not there, but he told me that he had gone to the rally and that Mr. Krajisnik attended this rally, but I know nothing else about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that this rally was organised by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, in the second half of 1991, to your knowledge, were there any military training which would be participated only by members of one ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. In the village of Ukrinica, there was in so-called Territorial Defence training, and it was only for Serbs. And there was one Bosniak who took part in that training. All this lasted until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who organised this military training? Did you know any of the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I knew men who were instructors, that is, Mr. Simic, a teacher; and Mr. Jotanovic, Mr. Marinko Jotanovic; and Vlado Munic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that this Simic, that he was a teacher, and Marinko Jotanovic -- was Marinko Jotanovic a teacher as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. I don't know what his profession -- what his occupation was, but he was a Captain 1st Class in reserve. That was his rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So both were reserve officers, and as reserve officers, to your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as reserve officers, to your knowledge, were they authorised to launch such trainings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you yourself was a commander of the Territorial Defence unit. You were a reservist; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was not a commander. I was a reserve senior officer, as the commanding officer of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when you were a member of reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was a member until 1989. I do not recall the date. It was October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you to confirm the year again? Did you say 1989 or some other year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you mentioned October 1991 as time when you received a letter that you were discharged from the military service. Is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I, in relation to the demobilisation, I was speaking about October 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not correct that you would be discharged from the military reserves in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I don't recall that in 1991. I don't recall it as being in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you one more question in respect to military. Did you notice that during the time of 1991/beginning of 1992, that respective ethnicities would arm themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I noticed that in 1991 and in 1992, Serbs were being armed. I mean, there was training and they were given weapons. They were given arms, automatic weapons, hand grenades. They would return from this training in Ukrinica. Sometimes they would be drunk and on the way back there would be some shooting around the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Serb civilians carrying openly weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did you see any weapons which would be carried by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that you saw helicopters flying above your village. When was it, and where these helicopters landing on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: That was in May 1992, and they flew over our villages. They landed in the village of Djulici, where there was barracks, military barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it normal that these helicopters flew above your village? Because you mentioned that in Djulici there were military barracks. Or was it something exceptional?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: It wasn't unusual, because every military helicopter that flew over the villages, I mean, we were not concerned. We were not afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now I would direct your attention to the town of Teslic, and I want to ask: Do you know who was the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: His name was Nikola Perisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that an organ called Crisis Staff was established in the town of Teslic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you heard the term either "War Presidency" or "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I heard about the terms, both "War Presidency" and "Crisis Staff," but I wouldn't know who organised that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or did you learn at any stage names of someone who would be a member of this War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I only knew about Mr. Perisic, because he had been the head of the Teslic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned some other names of men of authority from Teslic. Do you still remember the people who were -- who held the important positions in the Teslic town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I remember the people, but I don't know whether they were members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we are talking about, let's say, April 1992, April/May 1992, do you know who was chief of SUP or -- I'm sorry - who was the chief of the SUP in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: His name was Dule Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you stated, is it correct that you didn't know whether he was a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. Is Dusan Kuzmanovic and Dule Kuzmanovic the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is Dule Kuzmanovic. That was how people called him. But whether he was Dule or Dusan, I don't know. I knew him as Dule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any checkpoints, either in your village or in surrounding villages, during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. They were in my village, at the entrance to the village, in Muslim houses. There was the Serb checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you more or less answered the question. Who manned these checkpoints? Were they policemen, military men, or who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: These were soldiers in multicoloured uniforms. Now, whether they were policemen, I don't know. They didn't have insignia that I would be able to tell apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they of Serbian ethnicity, Bosnian ethnicity, or were they a mixture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I knew from among them only Bozimir Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about surrender of weapons. Did you hear any announcement, either over radio or conveyed personally, that people had to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: There was an announcement on Teslic radio. It was an order to hand over weapons, that all citizens of Teslic municipality should hand over their weapons by the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, by any chance, know whose order it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: On the order of Mr. Perisic. That was the announcement said on the Teslic radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this order was for all the citizens or only for some ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: All the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you supposed to hand over these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: To the Territorial Defence staff in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any weapons in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: There were sporting, hunting rifles, and some people would have a pistol, legally owned pistols with permits. And there was sporting rifles, hunting rifles, people who were hunters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, to your knowledge, did everybody hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: As far as my village is concerned, hunting rifles and pistols were all handed over, because I also had a pistol and I handed it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from someone that there would be some villages which wouldn't hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could refresh your memory again: Reading from your statement, you stated that hoping to avoid the fate of some other villages which had come under armed attack, such -- "Rajseva, Kamenica, Stenjak, Komusina, Slatina, Studenci, and Hrankovic, I too handed over my pistols." Why this listed villages were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to that statement. It calls for speculation on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If he has information, it seems that they reached a decision in his village to hand down -- hand over the pistols, precisely of knowledge that they had about attacks in these villages having occurred previously. So if they had information on those attacks, perhaps he also had information on why those villages had been attacked. So Madam Richterova, I suggest that you put the question again, because in the meantime, I may have distracted the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I will do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I listed you names -- I listed you some villages, and you stated: To avoid the fate of these villages, we handed over my pistol. How -- what was the fate of these villages, and why these villages were attacked, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you stated: Hoping to avoid the fate. So there had to be something behind your decision. If you can explain to us why you -- why you stated this in your statement. Of course, if it is not true, tell us it's not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: and therefore -- no, no, no, but we still have to take action, because the -- we are not in private session, so there is a transmission. And what the public would hear, albeit distorted, there would still be his name. And therefore, we are ordering that his name will be redacted from the transmission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the interpreter didn't mention the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but what I mean to say is this: That whoever will be following the transmission with the 30-minute delay would be hearing the distorted voice of the witness in Serbo-Croat, presumably, and the fact that it is distorted would not eliminate the mentioning of his name if his name was indeed mentioned. So what I'm asking is that, taking advantage of the 30-minute delay, that part of the transmission where the witness, in his own language, mentions his own name, be deleted or not transmitted. Have I made myself understood or does it create problems? Yes, but I want to know, because no one is telling me whether it's clear or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm told that there is some technical difficulty because the technicians themselves are not in a position exactly to distinguish where the name was mentioned. So they are going to do is they are going to obliterate a chunk where they assume -- actually, the witness's answer. I'm just informing you of that, and we can proceed. In the meantime, sir, please try to help us. Don't mention your own name ever. We are trying to protect you, but if you mention your name, others will hear it. And also, if by any chance you are referring to members of your own family or close friends who used to live near you, neighbours, don't mention their names. Otherwise, if you need to mention the names, tell me so and we will go into private session, and that would make it possible for you to mention the names, because no one would hear them. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you were arrested by four soldiers or four men in uniforms. Would you be so kind and describe their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: They were multicoloured uniforms, multicoloured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether they wore any belts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, they had belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: One of them had a white belt, and the others had the kind of belts that were worn by the former JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I suppose they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were taken to Gornja Radnja. Where in Gornja Radnja you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: They took me to the youth centre, which was also the seat of the local commune, and that is where the headquarters of their command was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were arrested, were you handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: They wanted to tie my hands with a piece of rope while I was being driven to Gornja Radnja. I didn't allow them to do that, and they didn't tie me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Gornja Radnja, who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I arrived at their command there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: The commander, Nedeljko Subotic, also known as Bombas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with this Nedeljko Subotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: There was Marinko Jotanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Nedeljko Subotic. Did you know his name at the time you met him, or did you learn his name at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I did not know at the time what his name was. I learned it only later. And as for Marinko, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you arrived to Gornja Radnja? Were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated. It was the commander, Subotic, who interrogated me. He told me that according to a letter that they had, there were 15 guns and three machine-guns in my village, and I answered to that that this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: A man called Dragan hit me. He is from Podnovlje, a village between Doboj and Modrica. The name of that village is Podnovlje. I don't know how far that -- the distance between these places is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that this one Dragan hit you. During the interrogation, were you hit only one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. I was hit several times. My nose started bleeding and I also started bleeding from my mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it only Dragan who participated in beating you, or was it also this Subotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Only Dragan and another soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long this interrogation lasted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: An hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the interrogation, at any time did you lose your consciousness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. When I was beaten, I lost my consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they use any objects to beat you or just their arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was kicked, I was clubbed, I was hit with something that looked like a baseball bat, made of wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that this interrogation lasted for about one hour. What happened after this one hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was put in a Golf car. I was handcuffed and I was taken to Djulici, to the school there, which housed the command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the person who took you to Djulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I remember. It was Dragan from Podnovlje and Marinko Jotanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken in Djulici. How long did you stay in Djulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: To Pribinic, and there was a camp there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness some photographs. I can provide the photographs. Their Exhibit numbers are P1955.1 until .10. Can you just place them one by one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could, sir, tell us whether you can recognise any of these pictures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I can see the building in Pribinic which housed the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I would like the technicians to adjust the field of view in a way that I can see the exhibit number and ERN number, please. Yes. Perfect. So the witness, for the record, the witness has just been referred to and answered a question related to Exhibit P1955.1, with ERN number 0219-4087.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe this building? Where is the entrance, and where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: The entrance is here. This is the entrance. Here you can see it. There was a storage here, and behind this door there was another door, and we would go through that door to the storage, and this is where we were kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what there was before in this -- what this building was used for before it was turned into the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Before the war, this was a store which sold agricultural chemicals and things like that, and we used to call it Apoteka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see another building adjacent to this red/yellow building. What was that building used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: This other building adjacent to the first one used to be a post office, and the military police that guarded the camp was accommodated here. And this used to be a solitary cell. Everybody who was brought here would spend two or three days in this solitary cell in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am done with the photographs. We were lucky. Immediately the first photograph was the right one. Yes, we are done with all the photographs. Sir, after you were taken to Pribinic, did you know who was the camp commander of this prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Dragan Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Babic from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He worked in Masinstvo, so I did know him from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you enter the camp, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that we redact: "He worked in Masinstvo," because that gives the impression that the witness himself had anything to do with that factory or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the witness has nothing to do with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we go ahead. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Where were you taken inside of the Pribinic prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was taken to this other part of the building, the so-called solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. I was still handcuffed when I got out of the car. Mr. Babic had a club in his hands, the one that I described before, and I was still handcuffed. He hit me four times on the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were hit by Babic, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Then he took me to this solitary cell. There was just one chair there. I sat down on that chair. Later on he came in. He gave me a piece of paper and instructed me to write down the names of those who possessed arms in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you write this information for Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I wrote down the names of those who had hunting rifles and sports guns, and those who had pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Dragan Babic satisfied with your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He was not satisfied with my list, and he started beating me. But he only kicked me on the back, and I lost consciousness after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you regained consciousness, did you stay in the solitary or were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in this solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I arrived on the 30th of June; it was a Tuesday. And I stayed until Thursday, sometime after noon. I believe it was around 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one question: This Dragan Babic, did he wear any uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, a multicoloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know whether he belonged to normal military or military police or just police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He was a military policeman, but he was a member of the reserve force. I believe that's what they called it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can recognise it according to name, but can you tell us what was his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in this solitary cell, did any of soldiers or policemen enter the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Only the guards entered the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The only person I knew was Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are still referring to Dragan Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a person named Dragan Panic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. Dragan Panic and Dragan from Modrica came to see me when I was transferred there. They came around 11.00 and they were drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they treat you? You said that they entered and they were drunk. What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Dragan from Modrica beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Dragan Panic participate in this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He just gave me two kicks with a bat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After spending some time in the solitary, where were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: They took me to the storage, where other people were, the place that I have just shown to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many other people were already kept in this other room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: There was Mujo Tenic, Hasan Iriskic, Pavle Grgic, Asim Skopljak, and Slavko whose last name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe us the condition in the Pribinic? And let's start with hygiene. Did you have toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: We had an outside toilet facility made of timber. It was some 20 metres from the entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a dry toilet, as called a Polish toilet, I think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. It was a makeshift facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I keep learning new things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have enough water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: We had water. We were not prevented from drinking as much water as we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to bathe yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you shave yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to change your clothes during the time of your confinement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. I spent 105 days there. I never had a bath, I never had a change of clothes. I never cut my nails. I never shaved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, what about meals? Did you have enough meals? How often did you receive your meal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: We received a meal between 3.00 and half past 3.00 every day. This was lunch. We did not have breakfast, we did not have dinner. The only thing that we received was lunch. We did not have enough food. And every time we went to take that one meal of the day, they would beat us and they would ill-treat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sleep? Did you have beds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. We slept in the storage, and we only had wooden pallets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe just the daily routines in Pribinic? Did you stay inside of the building the whole time or were you ordered to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: We stayed inside most of the time. Only younger people were taken out to chop wood for the bakery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many detainees were in the prison? Was the number -- did the number vary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: It varied. At times there were up to 25 or 30 of us; at times there were 15 of us; at times there were 7 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was released on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it -- would you be so kind and repeat once again the date when you were released, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: 5th of October, 1992, I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the whole time, can you estimate how many people altogether were kept in the Pribinic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I believe that around 200 people passed through that camp during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember names of any of the guards in Pribinic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I knew Babic. I knew Milivoj, whose last name I don't know. Then Miro Pejic, Mile Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are giving the names, can you slow down so the transcript can catch the names. So would you be so kind and start again the names of people who guarded you in Pribinic camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Dragan Babic, Milivoj, whose last name I don't know; Miro Bozic -- I apologise. Mile Bozic. Miro Pejic. Milorad Gojic, also known as Mico. Drago Kupresak. Ozrenko Gacic. Slavisa Kolobaric. These are the men that I knew. And there was also another person, Zoran Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's stop here for the time being. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just didn't sit down quick enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes, Ms. Richterova. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before the adjournment, you gave us the name of people who guarded you in the Pribinic camp. Were all these men members of -- to your knowledge, were all these men members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all of the Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Just Babic. Not the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you learn their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: During that time while I was there, they would be calling each other, so that's how I picked it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time of your detention, were you told why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with any crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you or other detainees interrogated during the stay in the Pribinic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the interrogation? Were they the same people who guarded you or were there some other people who did the questioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: The questioning was led by Aleksa Jovic, deputy commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only Aleksa Jovic was the person who interrogated you, or was there somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: While I was there, he was the only one who came, on a couple of occasions, to interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you mentioned Drazenko Kupresak as the person who most frequently did the questioning. Is it correct or is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this Drazenko Kupresak was one of the men who was among the guards in the Pribinic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Drazenko was a guard. He did not interrogate. Aleksa Jovic came to interrogate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how were you treated during your stay in the Pribinic? We already heard about the condition under which you live in the camp, hygiene, et cetera, but how were you physically treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Every morning, Dragan Babic called for us to get breakfast, but instead of breakfast, we would be beaten up, all of us, one by one, no matter how many people there were in the camp at one time. Everybody would be beaten up, every single morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it only Dragan Babic who beat you, who did the beating, or did other guards participate in the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Others too. Milivoje and others. All of them, if Babic wasn't there, then the same thing would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you mentioned that you developed pneumonia. Were you provided with some medical aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. There was some medical help. I was taken to the hospital in Pribinic. There was Dr. Rade Kalamanda who was there. He examined me and he diagnosed me with pneumonia and prescribed me five shots of penicillin. And every day I would go and be administrated penicillin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else sustain some injuries or develop some disease for which he would need to be medically attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: There were a lot of people who were injured, Mustafa Dzafic, for instance, Petar, whose last name I don't know, also known as Pero. These people were injured. They had been beaten up. And they ended up having infections and they died. And also Remzija Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from you, did anybody else receive any medical help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Only Mujo Tenic, because he had had a shotgun wound in his leg, and he went with me every day to have his wound dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your stay, to your knowledge, did anybody die in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Before I arrived, there was Asim Skopljak, who had been brought for 25 days before me, and he told us then three men had died. Two of them he didn't know, and one of them, called Semso, also succumbed to his injuries. He was arrested the same time as he was. He was from Topcic Polje, near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the deaths of these three men you learned from this person, Asim, did you personally witness any killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: For these three men, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking about these three men. I just stated that you learned about these three men from Asim Skopljak. But you personally, after you arrived to the camp, did you witness any killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Mustafa Dzafic succumbed to his injuries. Pero, from the environs of Kotor Varos, he was a person who was retarded mentally. Then another man called Petar. Then Juro Erejz, then Remzija Jasarevic. That's five people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just now briefly, if I ask you to go through these killings and state what you saw personally, how these people were killed or how these people died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: They were inflicted injuries, arms and legs, and they developed infections; and because of that, they died. As far as Pero is concerned, who was mentally retarded, I went out with him to clean the compound, to clean the cigarette butts in front of the offices where the military police were. And then Milivoje whose last name I don't know, approached us. He was holding a metal bar and he approached Pero, hit him on the side of his back and head, hit him once. And Pero fell. And then I lifted him up. I poured some water over him. That's what Milivoje ordered me to do. And again when Pero got up, he didn't collect cigarettes butts. Again he was hit again. And then Pero fainted. Again I poured water over him and I went to look for help so that if somebody could help me to bring him into the room where we were. The next day, Pero died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned another person called Petar. This Petar is different from this Pero, this mentally disabled man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Pero is mentally retarded, and Petar is a different person, from the area of Zepak, between Sera and Zepca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this Petar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He also had been beaten up. He fainted and was out of it for two days, and then he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness his killing personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Well, I was there when they were beating him up and when he lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still remember which of the guards participated in beatings of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Milivoje, whose last name I don't know, and Dragan Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you mentioned Mustafa Dzafic. How did Mustafa Dzafic die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Mustafa Dzafic had an injury inflicted. There were three soldiers that entered. I didn't know them. They hit him a couple of times on left or right arm; I don't recall that. And Dzafic also suffered a kind of sepsis, an infection of the arm. He was a medic by profession. He asked for medical help. They didn't let him have it. And after that beating up, four or five days later - I don't recall exactly, because a lot of time has passed - Dzafic succumbed to his injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that three soldiers unknown to you entered, and I presume that they entered the room in which you were kept. Are you talking about regular soldiers or military soldiers, or are you talking about military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: These three soldiers I didn't know them. They didn't come here to be guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further, you mentioned Juro Erejz. Can you tell us how this person died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Juro Erejz arrived in the evening, in front of this place where we were. He was beaten. I didn't see them. When they beat him up real good. Then they put him in the room where we were. That was in the evening. It was dark. There was no electricity. And in the morning, when we woke up, he had all bruises all over his body, on his back, on his kidneys, and in the evening we went to the toilet, and in the course of that -- in the course of that evening, Erejz died on his back -- on his way back from the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who beat him, who did the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see it. That was happening in front of our door. That's why I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you at least aware whether the beating was done by the guards or, again, people who came from the outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He told us in the morning that he had been brought in a van, that there were -- these were different people. I don't know. Really, I can't describe something I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you stating that he was arrived -- he arrived to the Pribinic already in the state that he was beaten on previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they continue to beat him also after he arrived to the Pribinic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I said they arrived. He was beaten when they brought him. And he immediately died the following day. He slept that night, and the next morning, the next day, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned Jasarevic, Remzija Jasarevic, as another person who died in the Pribinic camp. Can you tell us how this person died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Remzija was brought. He was in the cell much more than we were. When he was brought there, he had already been beaten up, and when he arrived, he was further beaten by Dragan Babic, by Milivoje and by a man who called Srbijanac. I don't know this young man. He was tall. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these five persons you witnessed as being killed are all which -- who were killed, whose deaths you witnessed personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you learned about three other men via Asim Skopljak; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any time that the International Red Cross would come to the Pribinic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. We would feel if something was happening. I know that people would be looking for us, and then we would be transferred to the cellar of a school nearby. We would be hidden in the basement. Sometimes we would spend ten hours in the basement, sometimes at night, from the evening until the morning, and then they would return us back to the camp. I never saw that we were visited by anybody from the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Dragan Babic ever replaced from his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Aleksa Jovic came in his place. He took me and Ibrahim Ceric out and he asked us: Who has been beating you the most? Just tell me freely. We said that we were beaten most by Babic, by Zoran Markovic, and by Milivoje. The next morning already they were replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did replace them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I presume that Aleksa Jovic was the person who replaced them. I don't have any other idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, you mentioned two names, Stojan Radic and Mile Marjanovic. Do you remember these names and whether these persons ever worked in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. Stojan Radic was a deputy. He was a deputy to Milorad Gojic, also known as Mico. While Mile Marjanovic was carrying out the duty -- I wouldn't know exactly. I mean, he's the one who spared us. For instance, when we would go to the toilet, we wouldn't have to -- we wouldn't have to put our hands on our head like this, but we would normally walk, with our hands down. But with everyone else, we would have to put our hands up on our head and return like that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you -- after Dragan Babic and other men were replaced, did the maltreatment continue or was everything in order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: The same continued. The same people came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some guards were replaced, and now you are stating the same people. What do you mean, stating the same people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I mean the same people who replaced those guards, they continued with the mistreatment and the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did -- do you know the name Predrag Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. Mr. Predrag Radulovic came to our camp. I don't exactly know the date. We were standing facing the wall, with three fingers raised. That's how we were standing. A person came in, a civilian. He said: Turn around and hello. And we turned. He said: Sit down. So we sat down. He introduced him. He said: I'm Predrag Radulovic, also known as Pile. I have established civilian authority in Teslic, and the camp will be disbanded on Monday. It was Saturday when he arrived. After that, he never came and we never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I know that it is -- it happened many years ago, but would you be able to tell us in which month Predrag Radulovic arrived to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I think that was at the end of July. I don't know the date. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you already stated, you were released from the camp on 5th of October, 1992, and you were exchanged; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were -- you also stated that you were maltreated in the camp. Can you very briefly tell us whether you developed any medical condition after this beating which would sustain until these days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes. I had injuries on my back, and I have a problem with my foot. I have trouble walking. When I walk, it would frequently happen that I actually fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you one document. You have already seen this document during the proofing, and I would like you to make a comment on the content of this document. It's -- the exhibit number is P1941.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we could place the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, I am referring to the third paragraph, starting on the fourth line, and I will read it slowly in English. And I want from you to tell whether it reflects accurately the situation as you experienced: "They had aided --" the first paragraph, or the first line, is talking about people like Srdjan Marjanovic, Sladjan Covic, Zoran Jorgic, et cetera, and the text continues: "They had aided the Mice group in perpetrating crimes, and after the Mice were arrested, the said group of military policemen, under command of the company commander Srdjan Marjanovic, without leaving any written traces, continued to arrest large numbers of Muslims and Croats, detained them in the military prison in Pribinic, and then disappeared without trace. After establishing the military prison in Pribinic, no written orders for arrest or detention access, no for the reasons for the arrest or detention of any person, apart from cases when this SGB carried out -- SJB, I'm sorry, carried out the criminal investigation." And then it follows, says: "It is assumed that over ten persons in Pribinic military prison were killed in the most cruel fashion by severe beating. The organs of the military police never brought any criminal charges for any criminal activities against these persons." This document is dated 22nd of September, and before I ask my question, I only want to state that this official note is attachment to a letter which is under Exhibit P1942, and that letter follows in your binders this official note. And I must say that, unfortunately, another document was wrongly copied as attachment to this letter. You can see from the logic of things that the document which is wrongly attached is -- ERN number is 0110-4838, has nothing to do with the content of the letter dated 29 of September, 1992. So I would appreciate if you could disregard the document of the stated ERN number. Now, sir, as I read the part of this official note and you managed to read it as well, does it reflect accurately what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this document. This is dated 22nd September, 1992. I was in Pribinic at the time, and I am not familiar with this. I am not familiar with the people who are mentioned here. These people were not brought there while I was there. I mentioned the individuals who were killed, and as for these, I'm not familiar with any of these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't listen to my question. I was only asking whether the fact that people were arrested and detained in the Pribinic camp is correct information, and the fact that people were killed in the Pribinic camp is correct information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: These are the facts. I told you a little while ago that people were killed. But I don't know anything about this document, and I certainly can't speak about things that I don't know anything of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one more question. I'm sorry. I'm done with this document. I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time of your detention, have you -- did you hand over or were you asked to hand over any money, any valuable things to any of the guards in the Pribinic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: People who were brought to Pribinic -- for example, I, when I came, I had a watch and an ID card. These were taken away from me and never returned to me. I personally did not have any money on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, to your knowledge, was any valuable taken from your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. My house was torched, together with all the things inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, if I may refresh your memory: You stated that the keys from your car had to be handed over to one Stojan Radic. Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it happen? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16985 to 16991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was in the Pribinic camp, and my car, Zastava 101, remained behind. I had bought it one year before the war. My car was in the garage. I don't know whether Stojan knew about that or not, but in any case, he came to my nephew, to my brother's son, and asked for the car keys. And the car keys were among the ashes of the house. We did not have the car keys. The garage was open, but there were no car keys. He broke into the car, and he managed to start the engine. He drove the car away and he smashed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Sir, you're going now to be cross-examined by Mr. David Cunningham. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. Cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I want to ask you some questions, and the first area of questions that I'm going to talk to you about involves the time period of 1990 to 1991. And to help you with the questions, I'll try to make them as short as I can. You told us that in 1990 and 1991, that there were changes that you noticed in the Serbs. Do you remember that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Switch off your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the same time period when the national parties were being formed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And each of the ethnic groups had their own national party. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you heard from a friend about a Serb rally in 1991. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, in your municipality, that the other political parties had rallies as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you attend, for example, any SDA rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to change the topics a little bit, because another area you talked about was how, in 1991, you noticed that there were more Serbs in uniforms in your municipality. First of all, do you remember talking -- telling us about that in your testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe in your written statement, that you started noticing the increased number of Serbs in the military and Serb reservists in your municipality in October of 1991. Does that time frame, October 1991, when you saw the Serb reservists and the Serb military in your municipality, does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The war with Croatia -- let me start again. By October of 1991, the war in Croatia was ongoing; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I did not make that my business. I only heard it on the media. But personally, I don't have any knowledge of that. But yes, I did hear about the war breaking out then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were not in the reserves at this time, were you aware of the fact that many Bosniak men had not answered the call to mobilisation? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that one of the things you saw during this time frame, in 1991, is that you saw Serb reservists in your municipality. First of all, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us that you knew that there was at least one Bosniak who was joining in the training sessions in your municipality. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it is that only one Bosniak was involved in these training exercises? If you know, it's fine; if you don't know, it's fine too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that there was a military prison in Pribinic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that before you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was that military prison run by the military authorities, to the exclusion of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: The military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you now to around May and June of 1992 and go over some of your testimony during that time frame. You told us this morning in your testimony that during that time period, there was a demand made upon the local population to turn in their weapons. First of all, do you remember testifying about that demand this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things you testified to this morning was the fact that during this time period, in late May and early June of 1992, the military came and conducted searches of houses. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the individuals conducted -- when -- let me back up to make the question clear. When the military conducted these searches we are now talking about, there was no indication in your testimony that they destroyed the houses or abused individuals during their search. So here's my question: Did any of that happen? Did you see any of that happen, abuse to the citizens during the searches back in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I was talking about my village. As for others, I wouldn't know. I can't talk about other villages. I can only talk about the things that I saw in the area where I resided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I appreciate the distinction that you're drawing, but could you tell us what you saw, with your own eyes, in your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I've said that they came, that they searched houses, and that their behaviour was correct. They did not ill-treat anybody. They did not beat anybody. They did not take any things away. There was no looting, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics on you. I'm going to now talk to you about some of the events at Pribinic. One of the individuals that you told us about that was involved in the mistreatment of you and other individuals was an individual whose first name was Dragan, and he was from a village near Doboj. Do you know who I'm talking about when I refer to this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Dragan was a member of a group called the Red Berets, or did you ever see him -- let me just ask the first question: Do you know if he was affiliated with a group known as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in camp, in the Pribinic camp, did you hear anyone make any reference to the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone make reference to a group called the Mice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. While I was in Pribinic, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to talk to you about some of the events in July and August, while you were in custody in Pribinic. You testified to us this morning about an individual by the name of Aleksa Jovic. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- and I apologise for not turning off my microphone. What was your understanding of his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
