utterances.text: He was a deputy commander of the military police, but he was correct. At the level of Teslic municipality, while we were in the camp, and after I left the camp, Mr. Aleksa Jovic was very correct towards Muslims and Croats who resided in the territory of Teslic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He asked you about the beatings, who was responsible for the beatings. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong: He also said that he would try to take care of the people that were responsible for those beatings, to have them removed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was successful in having some of the guards removed, and Babic removed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a new commander that came in, Mr. Radic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not - and correct me if I'm wrong with this, but I believe your statement says you did not have personal dealings with him. You knew the deputy commander, Mr. Marjanovic, and I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the deputy commander like? Was he correct in his dealings with the inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, Mr. Aleksa Jovic didn't -- he was correct in the dealings with the inmates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he responsible for the release of any of the detainees, any of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he try to do anything with respect to securing your release from Pribinic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he try to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He tried to release me, but the attempts failed. He made promises to me, but they never came through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is from your statement, and I'm going to paraphrase it, and I want to see if it's correct. Because I believe you told the investigators that when it came time for your release, he told you: It might not be safe for you out there, because your house has been destroyed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you believe he was being truthful with you and being correct with you when he was talking in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final area that I want to talk to you about involves the individual by the nickname of Pile, Mr. Radulovic. Do you remember talking about him earlier this morning with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of his position within the government or -- within the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He came to the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I get the impression that he not only spoke to you, but he spoke to the detainees as a group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you, you and your fellow detainees, when he spoke with you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He told us that he would try and have us released on Monday, that he would disband the camp, that the civilian authorities were established in Teslic, that we were not guilty of anything, and that we would be released to our homes to continue working on our farms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise if you've included this in your answer, but did he also tell you that he was establishing civilian authority over the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radulovic, was he in a uniform or was he in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he talked -- and were the guards present? Could they hear his speech to you and the fellow detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he came to the camp, he told you that the camp would be closed, that you would be released within a few days. Did the guards agree, when someone in civilian clothes showed up and told the inmates, the detainees, that they would be released, what did the guards do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He left. What happened outside, I don't know. We remained inside, so I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, if you want to confront the witness with the relevant part of his statement, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And with the usher's assistance, I need to get his B/C/S statement from the Prosecutor. The relevant portion that I'm referring to is on page 10 of his English statement, and I unfortunately I cannot direct neither him nor the Court to the appropriate portion in the B/C/S. Your Honours, for the record, I believe it is the first complete paragraph on page 10 of the B/C/S version, because that is the one that contains the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't got the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise. Just to help assist Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what I'd like for you to do is you should have a copy of your statement in B/C/S in front of you, and I believe the first complete paragraph on page 10 of your statement refers to the events involving Mr. Radulovic. And what I would like for you to do is to read that paragraph to yourself, to use it to refresh your recollection, because I want to just ask you a few follow-up questions before I'm done with you. So will you let me know when you're done reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, look at me, please. You only are supposed to read the first paragraph, the one which -- in which you speak or you talk about Predrag Radulovic, just that paragraph. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Cunningham now is going to explain why what we have in this paragraph does not exactly tally with what you had just testified a few minutes ago. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question that I want to ask you is this, Mr. Witness: You told us today that Mr. Radulovic did not say to you and your fellow inmates that he was establishing civilian authority over the camp. That was your testimony. Yet when I look at your statement that you gave, you said that Mr. Radulovic said he was establishing civilian authority. Which one is it? Do you remember him saying it or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Switch off --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I said that he had established the civilian authorities in Teslic. He came in and told us that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me talk to you about my last area, because before you read your statement, I asked you about the guards' reactions to his statement that there was civilian authority and the band was being disbanded, and I believe my recollection is you said that the guards had no reaction. Having read your statement, in the statement you say that the guards reacted strongly to the statement by shooting in the air and spitting at Radulovic. Do you remember now what happened with respect to the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I forgot to say this earlier. Perhaps I may have made a mistake while I was giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to know where the mistake is, whether it's in the written statement or whether it's in his statement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think His Honour asked the question better than I ever could:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the mistake in your testimony today or is the mistake in the written statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Earlier. Earlier. The statement, the written statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't know if it's clear to the Court, but it's not clear to me. Did the guards -- do you remember the guards spitting at him and shooting their guns in the air after he talked to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a moment to confer with Mr. Ackerman, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have no further questions. Please have a safe trip home. I'll pass this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Is there re-examination, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have only one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Re-examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that this Aleksa Jovic treated you fairly, but you also said that after Babic was replaced, the guards mistreated you the same way as before. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever complain to Aleksa Jovic that the maltreatment or mistreatment continues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: We complained, but to no avail. Later on, Aleksa didn't come as frequently. He came rarely. So perhaps he was being prevented as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not have more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have some questions for you, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we could see that house you were detained in in Pribinic. I would like to see if you could see through the windows or were you kept in dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see through the windows, because there were bars on the windows. We were in the other room and the door was closed and locked. We couldn't see anything unless when we were going for lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: How long it was you were outside for lunch? What time did you spend outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: All that would happen in a building. We would eat in the room in front of the entrance, for the duration of the lunch, 15 to 20 minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So to be clear, did you spend any time a day, per day, outside that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. Only in the morning, going to the toilet, and in the evening, before going to sleep, then we would also go and visit the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And the rest you spent in complete dark; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question is: You were describing here for us that you -- at one time you didn't feel well and you were taken to the doctor and you received medical cure, and you also said that there was another man with injury, and he went with you and his wounds were dressed freshly. And you also told us that there was this young man. You described him as a student of medicine or a medic, Mustafa Dzafic, and that he, after maltreatment, he asked for the medical cure and he didn't receive any. My question is: Can you explain why those differences between you and that injured man and this young man, and others, were made, that you were able to receive the medical care and these people in very serious condition were not? Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I got pneumonia ten days after I arrived at the camp, and that is when I was given medical treatment. Now, whether it was after that that they were ordered not to give medical aid to anyone else, I don't know. Perhaps if it was a different period, later on maybe I would not have been given any medical help. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So it wasn't dependent on the people who were -- on the guards who were on duty. There were not better guards and worse ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. No. This was not dependent on guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have several questions. You testified that concerning to military training which began October 1991, 1991, for Serbs. Milovan Simic and Marinko Jotanovic were in charge of this military training. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said in your statement that, concerning this military training, they were obviously taking orders from higher military officers to conduct this training for Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What is the reason behind of this opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Because two people couldn't organise training of people without orders from the higher command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly "without orders from the higher command"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: What I mean is that they received orders from the higher command to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: That means that the orders from high-rank military officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: As for participants, almost all Serbs of military age participated, or only certain part of them participated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: These were able-bodied men who were to be trained, to be involved in this training, military training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is: Almost all Serbs of military age participated, or only certain part of them participated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Well, that's one part of that area where the training was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll try and rephrase the question myself, and you try to answer it, and answer just the question. You told us earlier on how, at this military training centre, a number of Serbs took part, and there was only one Bosniak. The Serbs that were undergoing training, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: That was the area that was covered by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we are obviously talking of Serbs who were of a certain age and could be engaged in such activities. Would you say that all the Serbs within this age bracket from your area were undergoing training, or only a part of the Serb population within this age bracket were undergoing training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What? A part or practically the entire Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I said those who were able-bodied from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you mean all of them or some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means yes. All of them, the great majority of them, or only a small part of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What should I answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, all right. We're talking of Serb able-bodied persons. Were there any left in your area of these Serb able-bodied persons that were not undergoing training in this camp, or were they all there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Well, those from my village, the Muslims from my village, didn't go to that training. But from my village, all able-bodied men went. I'm sorry. I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I think we've more or less --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My last question is: According to your knowledge, Muslims also began military training, or Bosniaks, in later stage, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No. I only said that only one Bosniak went to the training, to the military training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But I mean the military training organised by Bosniaks. According to your knowledge, Muslims also began military training, or Bosniaks, in later stage or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: In the area of Teslic, Muslims didn't organise any kind of military training, as far as I was aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a very few questions to put to you. The first one, I need a clarification from you. Do you recall earlier on you were asked whether you remember hearing announcements on the radio calling for the surrender of weapons? And you stated, answering a specific question, that you did hear such announcements and that they were directed to everyone. Now, in your statement to the Prosecution, you stated: "On the 29th of May, 1992, I began hearing announcements on the radio from Teslic for Muslims and Croats to hand over their weapons over to the Territorial Defence headquarters. The announcer said that by order of Nikola Perisic, all weapons in the possession of Muslims and Croats were to be handed over immediately and by no later than the 4th of June, 1992, and this announcement was repeated several times over the next few days on the radio." You will immediately realise that there is a contradiction here between what you stated to the Prosecution in your statement and what you testified today. Were the announcements directed to all, the entire population, or only to the Muslim and Croat component of the population? Which one of the two versions is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: It is true that the announcement was addressed to all the citizens of the municipality of Teslic, since it's the Serbs who responded and brought their own personal weapons, sports weapons, hunting rifles. The very same day they were returned, these weapons, while the Muslims and Croats didn't have those weapons returned. These weapons were kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, my other questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mentioned several persons in your testimony, and also in your statement. Dragan Panic, do you know if he's still alive, Dragan Panic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know where he lives, where he's living now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He lives in Gornja Radnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dragan Babic, do you know if Dragan Babic, the warden of the camp where you were ill-treated, maltreated, do you know if Dragan Babic is still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He lives in Buletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Miro Pejic, do you know if Miro Pejic is still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He's alive, but I don't know where he is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Zoran Markovic, do you know if Zoran Markovic is still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Gornji Hrankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And finally the person you referred to as Milivoje, Milivoje and whose last name you don't know, who came from the village of Liplje in the Teslic municipality, do you know if he's still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know where he lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Djulic [phoen]. He had a house built there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And finally, Drazenko Kupresak, from the village of Ruzevic, do you know if this person is still alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where does he live?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please turn off --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: He was in Ruzevici, but I don't know now. I have no information regarding him, whether he's working there or where he is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My last question to you: How long is it since you have engaged yourself in some kind of work, gainfully occupied -- gainfully occupied yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Last time I worked the 11th of May, 1992. That's when I received my salary, and never again. That's the last time I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And why haven't you worked again since the 11th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: Because it was on the 5th of October, 1992, that I went to the

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we redact this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to redact it. Yes, go ahead. Go ahead. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I forgot the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is, I asked you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you: And why haven't you worked again since the 11th of May, 1992. Now, don't mention again the area where you live now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I haven't been working. I have no employment. I am not working today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But are you capable of doing some kind of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: I have problems. I have two vertebrae that have been damaged in the spine. I have problems with my legs. I couldn't perform any kind of manual labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in receipt of any kind of disablement pension or subsidy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all from the witness. Sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony, which basically means that you can now return to your country, to your residence. You will be assisted by the staff of this Tribunal in whatever you need to make it possible for you to return without any delay. On my own behalf, and on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya, and also on behalf of the entire Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence. My last words is I join Mr. Cunningham and the others wishing you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you too. I thank to all of you for calling me here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the next witness, I suppose he is here already?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is. He's in closed session. Your Honour, I do have a number of matters which I think I ought to raise now, one ever which was raised by Mr. Ackerman this morning and you invited a response by the Prosecution. Is Your Honour intending to take the 25-minute break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I could certainly start the witness off at 1.00 but I'd like 15 minutes at the end to cover not just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not just the matter that Mr. Ackerman raised this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I say I invited the Prosecution for some kind of response, obviously if you want to give a response, because you don't owe the Trial Chamber a response. I can't expect it from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very much the usual response with an added, as it were, twist, but if Your Honours - we could start the witness at 1.00 - deal with preliminaries, and then perhaps adjourn. I can deal with the set-up of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Just to be clear, the next witness is 7.264; correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he enjoys --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session, yes. So make sure that -- I don't know what preparations you immediate to -- yes, I suppose so, but ... Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The understanding is, Ms. Korner, we start with the witness straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, and I'll deal with the preliminaries and then adjourn, if we may, the witness at half past 1.00. So the witness will stop testifying half past 1.00 and then I can deal with the matters at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And we are starting in closed session straight away. And I'm telling you this because of the technical difficulties that I was told of, and that's why we needed an extra five minutes so that they could have everything in shipshape order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1 (Redacted) 2 (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you raised the question of the letter which I understand was copied to the Trial Chamber that Mr. Ackerman sent to the acting director of OLAD, and asked whether the Prosecution had any comments. Your Honour, can I say this about what was said this morning: The Prosecution, at all times, has supported Mr. Ackerman's request for resources. I don't need to go over the reasons again. But he's argued very strongly that in order for this case to be completed with the expedition that Your Honours are asking for and that the Rules require, that the Defence should have proper support. Your Honour, that's clearly very much the case at this stage of the case, particularly in the light of recent events. We've already said to Your Honour that the next six weeks or so, until the conclusion of the Prosecution case - and I want to return to the time factor in a moment - is a time when really major witnesses, experts and the like, are anticipated to be called, and it's clearly, in everybody's interest that the Court, the legal aid and Defence unit, that Mr. Ackerman should get proper support. Your Honour, I cannot comment on the rate of pay that was raised, save to say this: It's not very different. We've made some inquiries from what it would appear the equivalent pay is for somebody of that level and grading within the Office of the Prosecutor. But the level -- the rate of remuneration is not a matter for us. All we can say is we do support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't expect you to, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the application that Mr. Ackerman has made that there should be an allowance for a case manager who can deal with the documents and who can obviously read both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner. The Trial Chamber directs that this part of the transcript, that is, Madam Korner's remarks on the subject-matter of the letter by Mr. Ackerman to OLAD be extracted and a copy of it given to Ms. Martinez, acting director of OLAD. Thanks. Yes. You may proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I then turn to a different topic, and that's the death of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've now had a better copy of the death certificate. Your Honours, unless Your Honours want us to respond in writing, we say here and now: We accept that this death certificate is a death certificate relating to General Talic. There was a full state funeral held on Saturday in Banja Luka, as we understand the matter. And unless Your Honours want it in writing, that is our view, and Your Honours can take the required procedures to mark the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't require it in writing. Having heard what you said is enough, and we will proceed accordingly to declare the criminal action extinguished causa mortis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Then, Your Honour, can I turn to Mr. Ackerman's response to the Rule 92 application that we made in respect of the witness from Celinac. Now, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman -- and Your Honours haven't ruled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not yet. We only got it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The reason I'm raising it now is because, if necessary, we will get him here for next Tuesday, because we understand that Mr. Sebire's cross-examination is not likely to take the whole of the session. So we're hoping to get this witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you mentioned the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just said from Celinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I said -- no. Mr. Sebire I mentioned. Mr. Sebire is the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Sebire. Okay. He's the -- all right. No problem. For a moment I figured out that you were mentioning someone who was protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Sebire is the investigator on exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is said about it is this: That it contains information that indirectly contradicts the statement of the witness who is about to testify. That may or may not be right, but it's on the statement, in any event. And in addition, the witness's statement contains significant exculpatory information which could be elicited on cross-examination. Well, it's there. As I say, Your Honour, we're anxious - and I'm going to move on to this now, the whole question of timing of what's left of this case - to try and complete the case, if not by the beginning of August, and I'm going to explain to Your Honour why I don't think that's possible. Shortly after the recommencement at the end of August as is possible. But it won't work. We're on a very tight schedule of the witnesses left. If we have to call witnesses like this for cross-examination. Your Honour, I'm making that point now so that Mr. Ackerman can hear it. And in our view, what is said is clear on the face of the statement, and unless there are other matters that Mr. Ackerman wants to adduce, we would suggest that it's not suitable to bring this man up for cross-examination. And Your Honour, what he does is simply add in further witnesses to the list. Your Honour, timing. We have to -- we've had to, as it were, redo the witness list again, because of problems with witnesses not being able to attend, and there's one witness, the one who we couldn't call, I think it was last Friday because of his illness, and it seems to us unlikely we can get him here in any event. If everything went according to plan, with no witness taking any longer than we have estimated, and with no delays, we would still find it very difficult to finish the Prosecution case by the 2nd of August. We've been told today that the expert witness for propaganda cannot testify between the 15th of July and the 1st of August, which is the last sitting day before the break. So, Your Honour, that is one problem, although that's a small one. But it does seem to us that we would really be pushing things, and we're cutting out as many witnesses as we possibly can to try and finish by the 1st of August. In addition to that, as I said to Your Honours, we will be disclosing, tomorrow, the statement for the constitutional expert. The documents, we hope, will follow shortly afterwards. Most of them have been disclosed but some haven't. But Your Honour, it's a hefty report and it's a lot of documents, and I think the same for most of the coming-up witnesses, the man with the diary from Banja Luka will be testifying, we hope, on the 16th of June -- 16th? Anyhow, mid-June. So, Your Honour, it seems to me that it's going to be impossible for, even with two counsel, but one who was just brought in, for this to proceed in the way that there's no gap at all. But, Your Honour, it may help if Mr. Ackerman can indicate -- I know it's difficult at this stage, but how long he thinks, if there is to be a Defence case, subject to any submissions of law made at the end of the Prosecution case, his case would take. Because I think that may assist Your Honours. I know that Your Honours -- that there is this timing problem so that the whole case has to be completed by the end of August of next year, but it seems to me, and I've had discussions with Mr. Ackerman about this, that the Defence case would not be running to an extent that it would make it impossible for the case to be completed by August. But, Your Honour, I'm raising it at this stage so we all have some idea of where we are. As I say, Your Honour, we were slightly taken by surprise to be told that there was this -- effectively this final date, if possible, and we're doing our best, but it's not -- I feel, going to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still not given us the breakdown of the witnesses that you still have. I'm still waiting for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, we have, Your Honour. We put in a motion which gave you the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it was filed sometime last week. It was attached to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. All right. Okay. All right. Okay. And this is what you stand by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, this is -- well, that is the best we could do, but there's been an alteration again, which is why we haven't given the Defence a copy, apart from the fact that it contains matters which, as Your Honour knows, we've -- are ex parte at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This in itself is not complete, no. I mean, for example, there isn't the name of the expert on propaganda, for example. I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. It was wrong. We corrected it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, that's the correction refers to this document. Oh, I see. I see. I see. That I saw yesterday and this morning, actually. There are two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But this was actually, I think, we did file this motion last week sometime, on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman -- have you finished, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I suppose two matters brought by Ms. Korner that call for some kind of comment from you. One is with regard to the witness from Celinac. Let's start with that. Do you require his presence here for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I set it in the motion, Your Honour. I think since we returned, I have filed responses on -- I haven't counted them up. 30 or 35 Rule 92 bis requests, and this is the only one that I have objected to in any way, I think. Certainly the only one I've asked to be brought here for cross-examination. So I don't think I'm being unreasonable about it. And it's one thing to say that it's in his statement, but, as you know, what's in a person's statement frequently doesn't reflect his knowledge, and it certainly can be elucidated upon, upon his presence here, which is what I intend to do with this witness. We saw today that what's in his statement doesn't necessarily reflect what the witness actually saw, heard, or remembered. And I don't know if it can cause the Chamber any concern, but it caused me a great deal of concern about the way statements are taken, as a matter of fact, that the witness would say: I absolutely said nothing of the fact. When it's something as clear as spitting and shooting. In any event, I do want that witness brought. Now, and of course it's up to Your Honours as to whether you grant that or not. The other matter which I can comment briefly on: I have looked in a little more than cursory way, and made a serious effort to try to make some kind of a reasonable prediction. I believe, Your Honours, that the Defence case is going to last somewhere in the neighbourhood of 15 or 16 weeks, which means that if we started in October, we could finish sometime around the end of February/first part of March, with the Defence evidence. And it may be less than that, but I think that's a reasonable appraisal of how long it will take. It's usual that Defence witnesses are quite a bit shorter in their testimony than Prosecution witnesses because of the nature of Defence testimony, basically. So I would think we could finish within that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll discuss this amongst us tomorrow during the first break, Judge Janu, and we'll come back to you. In the meantime, I'd like to know: The military evidence who has already given evidence in the Stakic case, how many days did he --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Stakic case, I think he testified for about three to four days. I'd have to double-check that, but I think it was something like that. Your Honours, I think -- we have him down -- we've given him four days for this trial. Your Honour, whether he requires all of those four days or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking. Because I see that he will be staying here a weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He works for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, he works here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's the one that Mr. Ackerman has been complaining about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he works for you and he is situated here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He works --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought he was situated somewhere across the Adriatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the best estimate we can give is two and a half days. I mean, in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness -- no, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was two and a half days in Stakic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two and a half days in Stakic. Because what I'm thinking of, Ms. Korner, and then we can talk about August as well. If we make use of Friday, 27 June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you see, there is no court, because we were planning to sit in courtroom 2, and that would have been court maintenance, but it so happens that now we will be shifting to the morning. We will be sitting in courtroom 3 and we can have that date available. We can fill it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why we've done some alterations to the list, because we've moved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And secondly, if one can anticipate reducing Mr. Brown's testimony to two days or -- I mean, he's already given evidence elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he gave evidence in respect only of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Prijedor is included also in our proceedings, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour. But he has to give evidence about what happened in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, let's discuss it first amongst ourselves tomorrow and then we'll come back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I hand to Mr. Ackerman at this stage so that he's not in the dark, and to Your Honours, because it's a different list slightly. It will probably undergo a change again, but if Your Honours look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll see that we've put in the witness for Celinac, but we do need to know, because we have to get him over here. He has to get a passport, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the position is a very simple one. If Mr. Ackerman requires the witness here for cross-examination, particularly on what he considers and describes as exculpatory material, then obviously the Trial Chamber cannot turn down that request. It has to accede to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't, but Your Honour I take the view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that there is case-law that says --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- theoretically we can, but I come from a jurisdiction where we would not even dare say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour -- in that case, is Your Honour ruling now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And in fact it actually can replace a written ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are deciding here and now that as far as the Rule 92 bis witness from the -- on Celinac municipality, referred to in Mr. Ackerman's latest response, a witness shall be brought over for cross-examination. Do you want to limit your cross-examination only on what you describe as exculpatory material, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what Ms. Korner suggested was that we could probably deal with that on Tuesday, because the cross-examination of Mr. Sebire will be quite short, I believe. So I think we can complete it that day without any limitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see he's gone into the 16th of June, but we need to -- if we can get him here, if he has a passport, he'll be here on Tuesday, the 9th -- 10th. So next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's it. We have to cut it short now, because we have already overstepped our limit. Is it something very urgent, Mr. Ackerman, or can it wait until tomorrow? All right. So once more, I thank the interpreters and the technicians and everyone else involved in these proceedings for your indulgence. We have again overstepped by about six, seven minutes. I thank you.
